problem: Existing VLN methods are trained in simulation and transfer poorly to the real world, while zero-shot LLM-based planners depend entirely on the LLM for decisions and ignore mature SLAM and navigation techniques. Existing datasets also mix object-centric and relative-positional instructions, so grounding of object-centric instructions cannot be studied in isolation.
motivation: Factor-graph landmark SLAM is robust and widely deployed (robot vacuums, drones), so aligning language instructions with it could give robust real-world instruction following. Instructions also encode a rough spatial layout of the environment (e.g. 'move forward until you see a chair'), which can serve as a prior map with uncertainty to be refined by observations.
key_idea: Use an LLM once, offline, to convert the instruction into a language-inferred factor graph of waypoints and landmarks with uncertain geometric priors, then refine it online with factor-graph SLAM as CLIP-matched detected landmarks are observed, and navigate to the inferred waypoints.
insight: Treating language as an uncertain map prior rather than having an LLM plan step by step gives better instruction following: nDTW 0.48 vs 0.33 for both baselines. The SR-OSR gap is smaller (20% vs 42-43%), so stopping is more reliable. Ablations show that oracle detection and oracle navigation raise SR from 0.58 to 0.70, so the pretrained detector and PointNav policy are the bottleneck rather than the graph formulation.
method: Language-inferred graph: GPT-4 with in-context examples decomposes the instruction into waypoints (SE(2)), landmarks (R^2), waypoint-waypoint actions and waypoint-landmark relations. These become a factor graph with Gaussian factors (e.g. 'forward' gives high x variance, low y and theta variance; initial mean displacement 2 m).

SLAM with map prior: MAP estimation jointly over robot poses, observed landmarks, inferred waypoints and landmarks. Landmark-observation likelihood factors reduce landmark uncertainty and thereby waypoint uncertainty; solved with GTSAM-style factor graph optimization.
Landmark perception: RAM for tags, Grounding-DINO for boxes, SAM for segmentation, giving observed landmarks and their features.
Data association: greedy pairwise matching of inferred landmarks to observations by cosine similarity of CLIP text features, with a threshold below which no association is made.

Waypoint selection: choose the waypoint minimizing squared distance to the robot plus alpha times the trace of its information matrix, trading off exploration and exploitation. Then sample a target from the waypoint posterior within the navigable region.
Low-level navigation and stopping: a pretrained PointNav policy (DD-PPO, HM3D) moves to the target. The robot advances to the next waypoint when within 0.5 m and stops at the last node.

New dataset (object-centric instruction following): built from GOAT-Bench/HM3DSem episodes in Habitat. GPT-4 extracts key objects from first and last frames, then writes object-centric instructions from the route's image sequence.

setting.backbone: GPT-4 (frozen) for graph inference; RAM + Grounding-DINO + SAM + CLIP (frozen); DD-PPO PointNav policy pretrained on HM3D
setting.training_data: none (zero-shot; uses pretrained foundation models and pretrained PointNav)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + depth, with odometry/pose for SLAM
setting.action_space: low-level VLN-CE style: move forward, turn left, turn right, stop (PointNav policy to waypoints)
setting.privileged: none (oracle detector/navigator used only in ablations)

numbers_note: The dataset's split name and size are not stated in the text; 'test' is an assumption. Metrics are printed as fractions (0-1), not percentages. Real-world results are qualitative only.
results: On the new object-centric instruction-following dataset, the method reaches SR 0.58, SPL 0.40, OSR 0.78 and nDTW 0.48. It beats VLFM (SR 0.33, SPL 0.24, nDTW 0.33) and InstructNav (SR 0.24, SPL 0.07, nDTW 0.33) on all metrics. It also runs on a Boston Dynamics Spot robot in an office.
limitations: Fails when multiple instances of the same object category exist (e.g. several doors) and when the detector misclassifies objects (television as fireplace).
Greedy CLIP text-similarity data association and a simple stopping criterion; no backtracking or recovery.
Only object-centric instructions (no regions), a small custom dataset, and only qualitative real-world evidence; no evaluation on standard VLN benchmarks.
